title: Parsing A Boolean Expression
statement:
The string `expression` is a well-formed boolean formula; evaluate it and return the result as a boolean. A formula has one of these forms:

- `t` stands for true and `f` stands for false.
- `!(X)` is the negation of the single formula `X`.
- `&(X1,X2,...,Xn)` is true exactly when all of the formulas `X1` to `Xn` are true (`n >= 1`).
- `|(X1,X2,...,Xn)` is true exactly when at least one of the formulas `X1` to `Xn` is true (`n >= 1`).

Operands are separated by commas with no spaces, and the input is guaranteed to follow these rules.
constraints: expression contains only the characters '(', ')', '&', '|', '!', 't', 'f' and ','
notes:
## Intuition

A group can only be evaluated once all of its operands are known, and its operands are known exactly when its closing `)` is reached. A stack keeps the operators and the finished values in reading order, so at each `)` the values on top belong to the group that just closed, with its operator right beneath them. (Recursive descent also works, but deeply nested input can overflow the call stack.)

## Approach

1. Scan `expression` one character `ch` at a time. Commas and `(` carry no information, so skip them.
2. Push every operator (`!`, `&`, `|`) and every value (`t`, `f`) onto `stack`.
3. On `)`, pop values while the top is `t` or `f`, recording in `hasTrue` and `hasFalse` which ones appeared.
4. Pop the `operator` under them. `!` gives `hasFalse` (its one operand was false), `&` gives `!hasFalse`, and `|` gives `hasTrue`.
5. Push the `result` back as `t` or `f`; it is now an operand of the enclosing group.
6. At the end a single letter remains; return whether it is `t`.

## Example 1, step by step

For `&(|(f))`: push `&`, skip `(`, push `|`, skip `(`, push `f`. The first `)` pops `f` (`hasFalse = true`) and then `|`, so the result is `hasTrue = false` and `f` is pushed. The second `)` pops that `f` and then `&`; with `hasFalse = true` the result is false. The stack holds `f`, so the answer is `false`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each character is pushed and popped at most once.
- Space: O(n) for the stack in the worst case.

## Pitfalls

- Operators and values share the stack, so stop popping operands as soon as the top is not `t` or `f`.
- `!` has exactly one operand: its result is the opposite of that operand, which is `hasFalse`.
- A recursive parser that recurses once per nesting level may hit the call-stack limit on thousands of nested groups.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `stack` | operators and evaluated values not yet consumed |
| `ch` | the current character |
| `hasTrue`, `hasFalse` | whether the closing group had a true or a false operand |
| `operator` | the group's operator, found under its operands |
| `result` | the closing group's value |
